items.title: Mistral launches Voxtral 3 voice agent SDK with real-time multilingual transcription, expressive speech synthesis, and deep tool integration for EU-hosted or self-deployed use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Voxtral 3
items.summary:
Mistral has introduced Voxtral 3, a voice agent SDK and speech model suite designed for real-time, multi-step conversations in over 50 languages. It combines accurate speech-to-text transcription, natural text-to-speech with emotional adaptability, and integrated tool calling to enable seamless workflow automation for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots. Voxtral 3 is available via Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment, allowing organizations to maintain data sovereignty and control over audio processing and retention.

The Voxtral 3 family includes state-of-the-art transcription models that support diarization and context biasing, outperforming competitors like Whisper and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Its text-to-speech models adapt voice emotion, pace, and emphasis based on conversational context across 35+ languages and 50+ dialects. The SDK enables agents to listen, reason, interact with business systems, and execute multi-step tasks during live conversations. A Pro Voice feature offers advanced voice adaptation using just 30 minutes of audio to replicate a speaker's distinctive style and emotional range.

items.title: DeepSeek releases DeepInfer, a high-performance inference framework for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models supporting NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
items.summary:
DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepInfer, a high-performance inference framework designed for large-scale production services using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash models. The framework supports optimized kernels, parallelism, asynchronous scheduling, deterministic sampling, and structured outputs, targeting NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs.

DeepInfer requires Linux, GCC 13.0 or higher, Python 3.12, and CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2 depending on the hardware. It provides offline inference capabilities with features like confidence-scheduled verification and batch-invariant inference. The release does not include a complete inference service, as components like KV cache systems and load balancing are needed separately.

items.title: Alibaba raises DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 output prices by 230%, input costs more than double overnight [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Alibaba hikes DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 output prices by 230%
items.summary: Alibaba increased the output price of its DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model from $0.40 to $1.32 per million tokens, a 230% rise, while input costs rose from $0.20 to $0.44 per million tokens. This sudden price hike reflects a broader trend of AI labs raising inference costs, impacting developers who rely on subsidized compute pricing. Other providers like Mistral and Alibaba's Qwen3.6 model also raised prices significantly, while Zhipu AI reduced prices on one model by 85%. The shift signals the end of heavily subsidized AI compute, urging builders to optimize token usage and caching to maintain profitability.

items.title: Researchers propose TTCS, a co-evolving test-time training framework that synthesizes curricula to improve large language models' reasoning on challenging tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TTCS: Test-Time Curriculum Synthesis for Self-Evolving
items.summary:
Researchers introduce TTCS, a test-time training method that simultaneously evolves a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver from the same pretrained model. The synthesizer generates progressively harder question variants tailored to the solver's current ability, while the solver updates itself using self-consistency rewards from multiple responses on both original and synthetic questions. This approach addresses difficulties in existing methods caused by overly hard test questions and limited test set sizes, which hinder stable model adaptation.

Experiments demonstrate that TTCS enhances reasoning performance on challenging mathematical benchmarks and general-domain tasks across different large language model backbones. The framework offers a scalable way to dynamically construct test-time curricula for self-improving models, with code and implementation details made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.22628v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-Time Training offers a promising way to improve the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) by adapting the model using only the test questions. However, existing methods struggle with difficult reasoning problems for two reasons: raw test questions are often too difficult to yield high-quality pseudo-labels, and the limited size of test sets makes continuous online updates prone to instability. To address these limitations, we propose TTCS, a co-evolving test-time training framework. Specifically, TTCS initializes two policies from the same pretrained model: a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver. These policies evolve through iterative optimization: the synthesizer generates progressively challenging question variants conditioned on the test questions, creating a structured curriculum tailored to the solver's current capability, while the solver updates itself using self-consistency rewards computed from multiple sampled responses on both original test and synthetic questions. Crucially, the solver's feedback guides the synthesizer to generate questions aligned with the model's current capability, and the generated question variants in turn stabilize the solver's test-time training. Experiments show that TTCS consistently strengthens the reasoning ability on challenging mathematical benchmarks and transfers to general-domain tasks across different LLM backbones, highlighting a scalable path towards dynamically constructing test-time curricula for self-evolving. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/TTCS.

items.title: WeAct introduces dynamic weight switching via capability-specific LoRA adapters as agent actions, improving Qwen3-32B accuracy by 6.2% over full fine-tuning and enabling modular continual adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
items.summary:
WeAct proposes a method for long-horizon agents to dynamically switch between capability-specific LoRA adapters during execution, addressing catastrophic forgetting by freezing the backbone and treating adapter selection as internal agent actions. This approach allows on-demand composition of capabilities within a shared context, improving performance across eight benchmarks.

In experiments with the Qwen3-32B model, WeAct achieved a 6.2% accuracy improvement compared to full fine-tuning and a 27.5% gain over the strongest static LoRA-merging method, while using less compute. The method also supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating adapters without altering the backbone or other adapters, enhancing agent flexibility and report quality.
items.description:
WeAct proposes a method for long-horizon agents to dynamically switch between capability-specific LoRA adapters during execution, addressing catastrophic forgetting by freezing the backbone and treating adapter selection as internal agent actions. This approach allows on-demand composition of capabilities within a shared context, improving performance across eight benchmarks.

In experiments with the Qwen3-32B model, WeAct achieved a 6.2% accuracy improvement compared to full fine-tuning and a 27.5% gain over the strongest static LoRA-merging method, while using less compute. The method also supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating adapters without altering the backbone or other adapters, enhancing agent flexibility and report quality.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26847v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

items.title: OpenAI improves AI coding models for low-resource languages like COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic with higher accuracy and lower cost in software building and migration tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Advanced coding in low-resource programming languages
items.summary:
OpenAI has enhanced its AI models to better support programming in low-resource languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic, which are critical for banking, weather forecasting, and other essential services. The improvements focus on building new software and migrating existing code while preserving functionality, addressing challenges like limited documentation and legacy code maintenance.

The company developed two evaluations: MultiLangBench, which tests building a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 languages, and a COBOL migration evaluation that assesses code translation accuracy. The latest models, including GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, show significant gains in accuracy and cost efficiency compared to previous versions, with GPT-6 Astra achieving an 87.4% average pass rate on MultiLangBench and GPT-6.1 Sol reaching up to 97.9% accuracy in COBOL migration tasks.

These advancements aim to help developers maintain and modernize software in languages that underpin vital infrastructure, with OpenAI releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite publicly to support further development and assessment.

items.title: Researchers introduce VibeTraining-Bench to evaluate recursive self-improvement via co-design of training data, trainers, and inference harnesses across diverse AI tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
items.summary:
VibeTraining-Bench is a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents' ability to iteratively improve system performance by jointly optimizing training data, trainers, and inference harnesses, a process termed cross-component co-design. The benchmark covers tasks in terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning, with agents starting from identical initial systems and refining components under fixed resource constraints. Safeguards such as test data isolation and network restrictions are implemented to prevent reward hacking.

Evaluation results demonstrate that advanced research agents can significantly enhance target agent systems; for instance, GPT-6-Astra improved performance on the SWE-bench Verified task from 32.9% to 53.7%, nearing the 55.4% achieved by a human-developed instruct model. Despite these gains, the study notes ongoing challenges in achieving cumulative improvements through iterative co-design. The authors aim for VibeTraining-Bench to serve as a unified platform to advance recursive self-improvement and deepen understanding of cross-component optimization in AI systems, with code and data publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26342v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTraining-Bench.

items.title: Researchers introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework separating targets and updates in LLM-proposed repair actions, tested on traffic assignment and database repair tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
items.summary:
Researchers propose a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates the selection of records (targets) from the applied changes (updates) in repair actions suggested by large language models (LLMs). The framework measures the effects of correcting or retaining each component by combining proposed and reference targets and updates in four executions. It was evaluated on two tasks: traffic assignment, where affected demand is identified from road counts, and database repair, where affected rows are identified from aggregate reports, using injected faults and recovery rates to assess performance.

The study found that the value of a proposed update depends on the targets it is paired with; missed targets can hide useful updates, while excess targets may make milder updates more effective than reference corrections. In traffic experiments, retaining the proposed update on reference targets achieved 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, outperforming tuning update strength on proposed targets. In database experiments, replacing updates worsened some actions, especially those selecting unaffected records, with variation across models. A component-reuse study combining target-update pairings from two proposals improved the mean held-out recovery rate compared to selecting between original proposals.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26650v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) specifies which records to change and how to change their values. A failed action may still contain a useful choice of records or a useful update, depending on how the two are paired. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates selected records (targets) from the applied change (an update). Four executions combine proposed and reference targets and updates to measure the effects of correcting or retaining each component and their interaction. We evaluate the framework on two tasks: traffic assignment, where affected demand must be identified from road counts, and database repair, where affected rows must be identified from aggregate reports. An injected fault supplies a reference action that reverses it, and the recovery rate measures an action's loss reduction relative to that reference. For sparse-target actions in the traffic experiments, retaining the proposed update on reference targets achieves 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, compared with 43.7% from tuning update strength on the proposed targets. In the database experiments, update replacement worsens 17 of 108 actions, all selecting unaffected records, with sharply different frequencies across models. The value of a proposed update depends on the targets it is paired with. Missed targets hide useful updates, while excess targets can make a milder update better than the reference correction. In a component-reuse study, testing new target-update pairings from two proposals raises mean held-out recovery rate to 0.616, compared with 0.580 when selecting between the original proposals.

items.title: Researchers model service-induced GPU memory congestion in large language model serving, identifying instability and throughput loss mechanisms under high concurrency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving
items.summary:
Large language model (LLM) serving accumulates persistent GPU memory usage as each request's key-value cache grows with generated tokens, leading to endogenous memory pressure under high concurrency. When memory capacity is exceeded, active requests are evicted and restarted, causing wasted computation and reduced throughput. Researchers developed a discrete-time dynamical model capturing admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching, revealing that homogeneous workloads tend toward unstable eviction-free equilibria and converge to stable limit cycles with up to 50% throughput loss.

For heterogeneous workloads, the study proves a stability criterion and shows that workload diversity can desynchronize completions and stabilize memory-constrained serving. The findings identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability and propose scheduling design principles to sustain high throughput in memory-limited LLM inference environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.15555v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving, each request accumulates persistent graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during service as its key-value cache grows with every generated token. Under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage therefore increases endogenously over time: the service process itself creates future capacity pressure. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation and reduces throughput. We develop a discrete-time dynamical model of memory-constrained LLM inference that captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching. In the saturated-input regime, the system admits both eviction-free fixed points and limit cycles with evictions. For homogeneous workloads, we show that the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and that, except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique worst-case limit cycle that is asymptotically stable outside this exceptional set, with throughput losses as large as 50%. For heterogeneous workloads, we prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and explain how the survival-polynomial mechanism generalizes to multiple classes and heterogeneous-input lengths. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability. These results characterize when workload heterogeneity desynchronizes completions and helps stabilize memory-constrained serving. More broadly, we identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism and derive scheduling design principles for sustaining high throughput.

items.title: Researchers propose BridgeCast, a Transformer-based probabilistic model using conditional flow matching to correct biases in ocean wave forecasts by transforming them into reanalysis-like fields with exogenous atmospheric variables [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BridgeCast: Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables
items.summary:
BridgeCast is a physics-AI hybrid model designed to improve ocean wave forecasting by correcting systematic biases in physics-based models. It treats physical model forecasts as corrupted observations and uses a continuous-time generative process to align their distribution with reanalysis data, leveraging a Transformer architecture for spatiotemporal modeling and incorporating external atmospheric variables.

The model supports flexible inference through ordinary and stochastic differential equations and has been tested extensively on real-world datasets, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines across different regions and forecast lead times. This approach aims to enhance maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience by providing more accurate wave forecasts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.03759v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ocean wave forecasting is essential for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience, yet remains challenging due to systematic biases in physics-based models. Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast, within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times.

items.title: Researchers introduce reverse-geocoding-based location encoders that incorporate administrative boundaries, improving geospatial prediction tasks with a new RevGeoRQ architecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
items.summary: Researchers have developed a method to train location encoders that explicitly incorporate administrative boundaries and place names by using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised signal. This approach enhances existing location encoder architectures and improves their performance on downstream geospatial tasks. The team also introduced RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture optimized for reverse-geocoding supervision, which outperforms current location encoders on several benchmarks. The method provides more interpretable geographic representations through human-readable reverse-geocoded strings and semantic IDs, with code and model weights planned for release.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24306v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.

items.originalTitle: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
items.summary: Muse Glimmer introduces a 30 billion parameter causal language model designed for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware, integrating multi-step reasoning, tool use, and failure recovery without cloud dependency. It achieves state-of-the-art performance among similar-sized models on benchmarks for tool use, planning, and task completion. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, Muse Glimmer aims to promote open-source development of capable and safe local AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.24628v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

items.originalTitle: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
items.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often compromises their aligned safety behaviors, creating a trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Researchers propose WSR-Tune, a framework that reparameterizes weight matrices to concentrate safety-relevant information into a small subset of directions, which are then frozen during fine-tuning while other directions are updated for task adaptation. This approach reduces interference between safety and task objectives, enabling simultaneous safety retention and improved downstream performance. Experimental results demonstrate that WSR-Tune achieves a better balance between maintaining safety and enhancing task performance compared to existing methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26443v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often weakens their previously aligned safety behavior, creating an inherent trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this issue by identifying safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space. However, safety-related information is often distributed across many directions in this space, causing downstream updates to overwrite parameters that encode safety behavior. We propose WSR-Tune, a Weight Space Reparameterization-based fine-tuning framework that preserves safety during downstream adaptation. Our approach constructs a safety-conditioned basis and reparameterizes the weight matrices such that safety-relevant information becomes concentrated in a small subset of directions. We then identify safety-critical directions and freeze them in the reparameterized space, while updating the remaining complementary directions for downstream adaptation. By explicitly structuring the parameter space to disentangle safety and task information, our method reduces interference between objectives and enables simultaneous preservation of safety and improvement in downstream performance. Experimental results show that our method achieves a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable LLM fine-tuning.

items.title: Alter launches privileged access management platform for multi-user AI agents with per-agent keys, policy enforcement, and audit trails [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
items.summary:
Alter has introduced a privileged access management platform designed for AI agents operating on behalf of multiple users. The platform provides each agent with its own identity and scoped credentials, enforces least-privilege policies, keeps credentials private, and maintains a tamper-evident audit trail of all actions. This approach aims to replace shared, over-scoped keys scattered across codebases with a centralized vault and fine-grained access control.

The platform integrates with over 140 providers and supports first-class integrations with LangChain, MCP, and AWS. It offers features such as credential vaulting, policy enforcement with default-deny rules, human approval workflows for sensitive calls, and real-time auditing that can be streamed to security information and event management (SIEM) systems. Alter also emphasizes security through encrypted credential storage, fail-closed authorization, and continuous monitoring, aiming to help teams meet customer security reviews and compliance requirements.

items.title: Navalia framework advances Cowork Agents with verifiable task synthesis and long-horizon post-training, improving financial analysis and general office task performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
items.summary:
Navalia is a new framework designed to enhance Cowork Agents—large language model agents capable of autonomous planning and complex task execution—by combining verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. It uses corporate financial reports to select evidence and build computation chains for analytical tasks, verified through independent LLM review and programmatic checks. The verified tasks support supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to improve long-horizon task execution.

Initialized from the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model, Navalia shows consistent performance gains across five benchmarks including OfficeQA Pro and Finance Agent Benchmark. The framework improves evidence integration, tool use, and task execution capabilities, and generalizes to broader Cowork settings beyond financial analysis, such as general office tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

items.originalTitle: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates
items.summary: Researchers have developed an autonomous construction approach combining a large language model and reinforcement learning to improve building efficiency amid rising housing demand. The method uses an enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm to plan mobile crane actions, supported by robot kinematics and control algorithms to execute tasks accurately. A customized embedding model extracts relevant environmental information, while ChatGPT 5 updates construction progress, provides safety information, and generates reports. The approach was validated through full-scale retaining wall construction experiments, demonstrating its feasibility for smart construction applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

items.title: Researchers propose multi-objective reinforcement learning method for LLM-based RTL circuit generation optimizing diverse Pareto-optimal solutions in power, performance, and area [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new learning method that uses large language models (LLMs) to generate RTL circuits optimized for multiple objectives—power, performance, and area—simultaneously. Unlike previous approaches that combine these objectives into a single reward, this method aims to produce a diverse set of Pareto-optimal circuits, allowing designers to select preferred trade-offs based on specific product requirements. The approach includes a generation-based training pipeline and a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution to measure each circuit's contribution to the Pareto front.

Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark demonstrated that this method improves relative Hypervolume by 13.3 percentage points over a baseline without PPA optimization and by 14.4 percentage points over single-objective reinforcement learning, while also enhancing circuit diversity. This advancement supports more flexible and efficient RTL circuit design by providing a broader range of high-quality candidate solutions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.

items.title: MedPAO-Assist launches edge-deployable AI for structured radiology reports using small language models on standard laptop CPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
items.summary:
MedPAO-Assist is an agentic AI framework designed to generate structured radiology reports from dictation and voice commands, operating offline with about 3.3 GB RAM and 31 seconds latency on a standard laptop CPU. It supports four imaging modalities—Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI—and uses a multi-agent Extract-Ground-Generate architecture with a small 0.6 billion parameter language model, enabling a fully voice-driven, no-keyboard workflow without internet connectivity or external APIs.

The system performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT ontology grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase. Hardware profiling and individual pipeline evaluations demonstrate its feasibility for real-time clinical deployment on CPU-only devices, addressing data privacy and offline operation challenges common in radiology workflows.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. The system currently supports four major imaging modalities -- Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI. To our knowledge, it is among the earliest agentic systems to run its entire pipeline with a Small Language Model (SLM) in the 0.6B-parameter range. This multi-agent architecture, built around an Extract-Ground-Generate paradigm, performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase, together forming a fully "no-touch" reporting workflow that requires no keyboard input, external API calls, or internet connectivity. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.

items.originalTitle: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution
items.summary: DataPraxis presents a new framework for synthesizing analytics tasks through verified workspace evolution, which progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings to uncover deeper analytical questions. This approach addresses limitations in generating tasks directly from raw data by verifying results during workspace evolution and task assembly. The team released DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified analytic trajectories across diverse domains and output formats, used to train large models DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves competitive performance on benchmarks like DABStep and JobBench, matching or surpassing models such as GLM-5.2. The dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. DataPraxis-5K is available at huggingface.co/datasets/stargazerhust/DataPraxis-5k

items.title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

items.title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.

items.title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

items.title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.

items.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.

items.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.

items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

items.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

items.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

items.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

items.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

items.title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

items.title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker

items.title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.

items.title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

items.title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.

items.title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

items.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

items.title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.

items.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.

items.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.
